newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Rivlin sees inflation risks.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Rivlin sees inflation risks.

text.p: The economy is slowing from its strong first-quarter pace but still faces the risk of higher inflation down the road, Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said Monday.

"We certainly have clearer signs that the economy is slowing, but we still have a tight labour market," she said in an interview. That means that the central bank will again face a "tough call" next month in deciding whether to raise interest rates further, she said.

After raising short-term rates in March in a bid to keep the economy from overheating and head off inflation, the central bank held rates steady at its last meeting in May amid hopes growth would slow.

That is what seems to be happening. Retail sales have fallen for three months in a row as consumers have cut back after a first quarter spending binge that powered the economy to its fastest growth in more than nine years.
Fed policy-makers are to meet on July 1-2 to weigh their next move and Wall Street analysts are betting it will once again be to to keep rates unchanged.
Rivlin said she did not think that the economic picture has changed all that much over the last few months, although the signs of a slowdown have become clearer.
"We still have these two things going on at once," Rivlin said. "We have an economy which is really slowing and we still have inflation risk. It could be that way for months."
Rivlin confessed that the current economic situation was "quite mystifying" but nevertheless welcome.
At 4.8 percent, the unemployment rate is at levels that in the past have led to stepped-up wage increases and higher inflation. But that has not happened this time.
"We have an inflation risk without inflation," she said.
She noted that many companies continue to report having trouble raising prices because of stiff competition from domestic and foreign rivals.
Besides the tight labour market, Rivlin pointed to the ebullient stock market as another area of possible concern.
"You have to be quite optimistic about (corporate) earnings to justify these kinds of (share) prices," she said.
With stock prices so high, there is risk investors will respond by sharply stepping up their purchases of consumer goods, spurring growth too much and fanning inflation.
"We haven't actually seen that," Rivlin said. But that could still occur in the future.
The Fed policy-maker, though, was generally upbeat about the longer-term economic outlook and saw no reason to worry about the economy falling into recession.

Although retail sales have ebbed in recent months, consumer confidence is strong, personal incomes are rising and employment is high, she said. "It looks like a very strong economy," Rivlin said. "The main risk is inflation."
